title: Qingming, sweeping tombs
hookLine: in spring, Chinese families sweep their ancestors' tombs

cards: A hillside in spring. Cars parked along the road, families climbing with brooms, buckets, bags of food and bundles of paper. A grandmother points the way.

A teenager carries a rake and looks at his phone. At a grave, everyone gets to work: pulling weeds, sweeping the stone, wiping the name clean so it can be read again. Then food set out, incense lit, a bow.
Sometimes a picnic right there, the living eating with the dead nearby. This is Qingming, the festival also called tomb-sweeping day.

teach.b: Qingming means clear and bright, and it falls in spring, when the weather is turning and the ground is green again.

It's a festival of the season as much as of the dead, which is why, in some places, people also go walking in the countryside or fly kites. The heart of the day is plain physical work. Weeds come out.
Dirt is cleared. The stone is washed. Some families add fresh soil to the grave or leave a slip of paper on it to show someone came.
Remembering is done with hands. Families set out food and drink the person liked and burn incense, and some burn paper offerings: folded paper money, or paper models of things the dead might need.
Customs differ from family to family and region to region, and some families today bring flowers instead. Why do it?

Confucian teaching speaks of filial care, the honor owed to parents, and the Analects ask that parents be served with proper rites while alive, buried with proper rites, and remembered with proper rites after.
Here's the other half: when life ends, the care doesn't.
It moves to a hillside, with a broom. People who keep Qingming hold its meaning in different ways, some as honoring spirits who are present, some as keeping a family's story alive.
Either way, the name on the stone gets read again.

how: At Qingming, Chinese families travel to their ancestors' graves to clean them, set out food, burn incense and paper offerings, and bow; customs differ by family and region.

games.q: you've climbed the hill with your family to your grandfather's grave. it's overgrown. what comes first?
o: leave quickly; the dead don't need tidy graves.
pull the weeds and wash the stone so the name can be read.
just take a photo and go.
games.why: the sweeping is the heart of it. then food, incense and a bow. remembering, at Qingming, is done with hands.

practice: Choose someone who has died, and think of one thing of theirs you have or could reach: a photo frame, a mug, a book, a pair of glasses.
If it's near, pick it up and clean it slowly; if not, picture yourself doing it, and let the cleaning be the remembering. If a memory comes with it, let it stay a while.

wordCard.voice: Qingming: clear and bright, the spring festival when Chinese families sweep their ancestors' tombs, bring food and remember them. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: sweep the tomb. Care for the dead can take the shape of a broom. Until tomorrow.
